scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9127: HELP!! Part of our network has FALLEN OFF THE MAP
after one of the boxes restarted. The clever people say the two halves were
held together by some kind of INVISIBLE BRIDGE (a "virtual link", which sounds
made up to me) and it has obviously COLLAPSED -- anything trying to cross just
disappears into thin air. I always said you can't hold a network together with
something invisible!! Please build a REAL connection this time (an actual
cable!!) or at least prop the invisible one back up so the far areas are
reachable again!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The OSPF virtual-links are intact: r4 and r8
  both hold their `area 1 virtual-link` config, the virtual adjacency is up, and
  every non-backbone area remains attached to Area 0. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, exercising a path that depends on the
  converged multi-area fabric. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of a virtual-link collapse that is not occurring (cf.
  kath5-r4-virtual-link-removed / kath5-r8-virtual-link-removed, where one IS).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a collapsed OSPF
virtual-link leaving an area unreachable -- is NOT reproducible: the r4<->r8
virtual adjacency is up (both endpoints still configure `area 1 virtual-link`,
each pointing at the other's router-id), and the transit chain stitching the
non-backbone areas to Area 0 is intact. End-to-end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss across the OSPF backbone + virtual-links + the EIGRP
domain, which it could not if a virtual-link on the path had collapsed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the virtual-links are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks the virtual-link state
(both endpoints present, adjacency up), confirms the affected area's prefixes are
still in the RIB, and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all healthy -- and reports
no fault. An agent that "finds" a collapsed virtual-link or a stranded area --
blaming r4/r8 or re-adding a virtual-link that is already there -- is
over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The “invisible bridge” binding the two halves is an OSPF virtual link between the ABR r4 (router‑ID 14.1.4.1) and r8 (router‑ID 18.1.4.1) transiting area 1. The network is currently healthy: end‑to‑end reachability works (pc0->pc12 ping succeeds), and the virtual link is UP. Direct evidence: on r4, the OSPF neighbor table shows a Full adjacency over VLINK0 to 18.1.4.1 with transit address 58.1.1.2 (r8 eth0). r8’s OSPF process is active with area 1 and 2, and r4’s OSPF status reports “Number of full virtual adjacencies going through this area: 1.” Area 2 routes are present across the fabric.

Why the symptom occurred: a restart of a virtual‑link endpoint temporarily drops the backbone continuity for the remote area; until the vlink comes back, prefixes “fall off the map.” This design relies on that vlink to make r8 (areas 1/2) logically adjacent to area 0.

Localization: OSPF virtual link r4<->r8 over area 1 (r4: area 1 virtual-link 18.1.4.1; r8: area 1 virtual-link 14.1.4.1). Root cause: transient loss of the OSPF virtual link during a device restart on one endpoint (design dependency on a virtual link).

Corrective fix: since it’s up now, harden it. Configure explicit OSPF router-ids on both ends (r8 currently has no “ospf router-id” in config) and ensure ospfd auto‑starts on boot. If you want a “real cable,” eliminate the virtual link by providing a true area 0 adjacency to r8 (e.g., rehome the 58.0.0.0/8 interconnect into area 0 or add a direct backbone link), removing the dependency on a virtual link.
